documents.searchText: _________________ _________________ 1 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Per Curiam SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES No. 26A560 MARKWAYNE MULLIN, SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY, ET AL. v. FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH, ET AL. ON APPLICATION FOR STAY [November 9, 2026] PER CURIAM. Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immi- grant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secre- tary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct bor- der barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” §102(a), 110 Stat. 3009–554, as amended, note following 8 U. S. C. §1103. The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary “ ‘to waive all legal requirements’ ” as “ ‘necessary to ensure expedi- tious construction’ ” of those barriers and roads, §102(c)(1), 119 Stat. 306, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifi - cally, the statute provides that “‘[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States’ ” and courts “ ‘shall not have jurisdic- tion’” over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A). Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102’s waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U. S.–Mexico border, in a region that U. S. Customs and Border Protection has designated the “Big Bend Sector.” The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional border barriers, and waived the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction. 2 MULLIN v. FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH Per Curiam See 91 Fed. Reg. 7298 (2026), as amended by id., at 40550; id., at 27969, as amended by id., at 34831; id., at 46939. Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organi- zation dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing suit in the U. S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the Secretary’s waiver determinations “violat[ed] the major questions doctrine under the U. S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1.” First Amended Complaint in No. 3:26–cv–01099 (WD Tex.), ECF Doc. 26, ¶¶75–85 (some capitalization omitted). Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secre tary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers. Ibid. On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a prelimi- nary injunction blocking the Secretary’s waivers and halt- ing all associated construction. The District Court acknowl- edged that its jurisdiction wa s limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents’ “major questions doctrine claim” qualified because, in its view, the “major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers.” Memo- randum Opinion in No. 3:26–cv–01099 (WD Tex.), ECF Doc. 75, at 7–8. The court further held that respondents’ “major questions doctrine claim” was likely to succeed on the mer- its because the Secretary lacked “ ‘clear congressional au- thorization’ to issue” the waivers. Id., at 8. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application re- questing either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court’s preliminary injunction. We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceed- ingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents’ so- called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Per Curiam labeled, respondents’ claim does not “ ‘alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,’ ” the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recog- nized that “claims simply a lleging” that the Executive Branch has exceeded its “statutory authority are not ‘con - stitutional’ claims.” Dalton v. Specter, 511 U. S. 462, 472– 474 (1994). That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plain- tiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional prin- ciples, including “constitutional avoidance, the clear-state- ment federalism rules, and the presumption against retro- activity.” Biden v. Nebraska , 600 U. S. 477, 508 (2023) (BARRETT, J., concurring). When courts invoke those can- ons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. See Clark v. Martinez, 543 U. S. 371, 382 (2005) (explaining that litigants invoke the constitutional-avoidance canon to vindicate their “statutory rights”). The same is true when a court invokes “the major questions canon of statutory interpretation.” FCC v. Con- sumers’ Research, 606 U. S. 656, 705 (2025) (K AVANAUGH, J., concurring). There is no such thing as a “constitutional” major-questions claim. The remaining factors also warrant a stay. To start, the District Court’s order, which bars the Secretary from exer- cising his statutory authority to waive applicable laws as he “determines necessary to ensu re expeditious construction” of border barriers under IIRIRA §102(c)(1), delays the Gov- ernment’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector. The injunction thus impedes the Govern- ment from advancing its “compe lling interests” in border security and integrity. Treasury Employees v. Von Raab , 489 U. S. 656, 672 (1989); see App. to Application 226a, ¶5. 4 MULLIN v. FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH Per Curiam In addition, the Government has presented a declaration from a U. S. Customs and Border Protection official, who attests that—because of the injunction—the Government is incurring nearly half a million dollars in costs per day, which “cannot be recouped” if it prevails at the end of this litigation. Id., 222a, ¶20–22. “[W]hile the loss of money is not typically considered irreparable harm, that changes if the funds cannot be recouped and are thus irrevocably ex- pended.” National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Assn. , 606 U. S. 998 (2025) (internal quotation marks omitted). The balance of the equities also favors the Government. Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress’s enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental- protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. §102(c)(1). And courts “of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute.” United States v. Oakland Canna- bis Buyers’ Coop ., 532 U. S. 483, 497 (2001). The Govern- ment’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recrea- tional, and environmental harm alleged by respondents. See Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 555 U. S. 7, 25–26 (2008). * * * The application for stay presented to JUSTICE ALITO and by him referred to the Court is granted. The injunction en- tered by the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas in case No. 3:26–cv–01099 is stayed pend- ing the filing and disposition of the Government’s petition for a writ of certiorari, if such writ is timely sought. Should certiorari be denied, this stay shall terminate automati- cally. In the event certiorari is granted, the stay shall 5 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Per Curiam terminate upon the sending down of the judgment of this Court. It is so ordered. JUSTICE JACKSON would deny the application for stay.

SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES No. 26A512 DAVID M. SCANLAN, SECRETARY OF STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE, ET AL. v. COALITION FOR OPEN DEMOCRACY ON APPLICATION FOR STAY [October 22, 2026] “This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower fed- eral courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.” Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee, 589 U. S. 423, 424 (2020) (per curiam). Here, the District Co urt did not point to any- thing that would justify deviating from that principle. See People Not Politicians v. Onder , 609 U. S. ___ (Sept. 25, 2026). Accordingly, the application for stay presented to JUSTICE JACKSON and by her referred to the Court is granted. The October 2, 2026, and October 5, 2026, orders granting preliminary injunctive relief by the United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire, case No. 1:26–cv–647, are stayed pending the disposition of the ap - peal in the United States Court of Appeals for the First Cir- cuit and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari, if such a writ is timely sought. Should certiorari be denied, this stay shall terminate automatically. In the event certi- orari is granted, the stay shall terminate upon the sending down of the judgment of this Court. 2 SCANLAN v. COALITION FOR OPEN DEMOCRACY JACKSON, J., dissenting JUSTICE JACKSON, dissenting. The Purcell case involved a federal court order that had completely enjoined enforcement of a state statute requir- ing voters to provide proof of identity when attempting to vote. Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U. S. 1 (2006) ( per curiam). Given the timing and the potential impact of that disrup- tive ruling, this Court said that lower courts deciding whether to enjoin an election rule in the lead-up to an elec- tion must consider the potential that the order itself might be harmful, insofar as it could cause “voter confusion” or create “incentive[s] to remain away from the polls.” Id., at 4–5. Importantly, this so-called “ Purcell principle” arose in a particular context, and this Court has yet to fully define its limits. It seems to me that a case involving a court order like the one at issue here—which left the state election rule untouched—does not necessarily fall within the ambit of Purcell and its concern about federal courts “changing the election rules” at the last minute. Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee , 589 U. S. 423, 424 (2020) (per curiam). Here, the District Court made a (certainly not clearly er- roneous) determination that correcting a publicized mis- statement about what New Hampshire’s election rules re- quire was necessary to ensure that certain citizens were not unduly burdened in their exercise of the fundamental right to vote.* So it issued a targ eted order, requiring only that —————— *In the District Court’s view, the plain text of the statute and all of the testimony submitted during three da ys of hearings—from both sides— demonstrated that the public statements and guidance that New Hamp- shire’s secretary of state was prov iding about the State’s recently amended registration and ballot-receipt requirements were, at best, mis- leading. See N. H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §659:13(I)(c) (Cum. Supp. 2025); §654:12(I)(d)(4) (2026); see also App. to Application for Stay 47a (“[T]he Deputy Secretary of State conceded that he did not see any factual reason 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) JACKSON, J., dissenting the relevant government official conform his public state- ments to the letter of state law rather than summarizing what the law required in a manner that could mislead vot- ers and local election workers. Consequently, here, the District Court’s injunction was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law. Under such circumstances, the relief the District Court provided actually promoted the interests Purcell sought to protect. When a federal court determines that material misrepresentations are being made about a State’s election rules, an injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem. Cf. Purcell, 549 U. S., at 4–5 (highlighting the risk of confusion “result[ing]” from “[c]ourt orders”). I respectfully dissent because—even, and perhaps espe- cially, when an election is looming—I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes. —————— why a student ID could not be reas onable evidence of a prospective voter’s identity under the safety valve included in New Hampshire’s voter identification regime” (internal quotation marks omitted)).

ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT No. 25–1098. Decided October 19, 2026 The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. Statement of J USTICE SOTOMAYOR, with whom J USTICE GORSUCH joins, respecting the denial of certiorari. In Chicago, a driver who fails to pay as few as two park- ing tickets risks forfeiting his vehicle to the city. The city then can do as it pleases with the vehicle, with no obligation to pay compensation, offset the unpaid ticket debt, or return any surplus to the owner if the vehicle is sold for a profit. See Chicago, Ill., Municipal Code §§9–100–120(b), (f ) (2026). The Seventh Circuit upheld that scheme as con- sistent with the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, rea- soning that it is “an exercise of the City’s police power to enforce its traffic code.” 163 F. 4th 411, 414 (2025). I have serious concerns about that conclusion, which implicates a Circuit split over whether, and under what circumstances, exercises of the State’s police power are immune to takings claims. Because that split would continue to benefit from further percolation, however, and because this case is not the best vehicle to resolve the split, I concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari. Chicago’s vehicle-forfeiture scheme is vast and lucrative, helping the city generate, according to one estimate, $264 million in traffic-ticket revenue (or 7 percent of the city’s operating budget) in 2016. See M. Sanchez & S. Kambham- pati, How Chicago Ticket Debt Sends Black Motorists Into Bankruptcy, ProPublica (Feb. 27, 2018), https://fea- tures.propublica.org/driven-into-debt/chicago-ticket-debt- 2 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. bankruptcy/ (archived at https:// perma.cc/K8MU-KVTW). Petitioners Ryan O’Donnell and Michael Goree are two of the many Chicago motorists sub - ject to that scheme. According to the complaint filed in this case, O’Donnell received two tickets for an expired meter and one ticket for time-restricted parking, totaling approx- imately $524. Goree did not have any tickets himself; ra- ther, a co-signer on his vehicle had approximately $560 of outstanding ticket debt from a different vehicle. After those tickets went unpaid, the city towed and impounded peti - tioners’ vehicles, adding additional boot, tow, and storage fees. It then sold O’Donnell’s vehicle for its scrap value of $273 and relinquished Goree’s vehicle to the lienholder. Neither petitioner received any compensation for the loss of their cars. Petitioners sued the city, alleging that its scheme facially violates the Takings Clause, which bars taking “private property” for “public use, without just compensation.” They asserted that §9–100–120 empowers the city to take vehi- cles “without providing any compensation to the owner or even a hearing to determine fair compensation.” Complaint in No. 1:23–cv–01192 (ND Ill.), ECF Doc. 1, ¶73. The Dis- trict Court dismissed the suit, see App. to Pet. for Cert. 16– 18; and the Seventh Circuit affirmed, see 163 F. 4th, at 414–415. As relevant here, the Seventh Circuit rejected pe- titioners’ argument that Ch icago’s vehicle-forfeiture scheme is like the tax-forfeiture statute this Court invali- dated in Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U. S. 631 (2023), for failure to return any surplus to the homeowner after a tax sale. The better analogy, the Seventh Circuit reasoned, was to Bennis v. Michigan, 516 U. S. 442 (1996), where this Court held that the government may seize property used in the violation of the law without providing any compensa- tion to the owner. See 163 F. 4th, at 414–415 (citing Bennis, 516 U. S., at 453); see also id., at 452 (forfeitures that 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. comport with due process do not trigger the duty of just compensation). Unlike the laws discussed in Bennis, however, Chicago does not impound only those vehicles involved in violations of its municipal traffic code. Rather, the city may impound any vehicle of a delinquent resident so long as ticket debts remain unpaid, regardless of whether the vehicle was in- volved in an infraction. §9–100–120(b). Indeed, that is pre- cisely what happened to Goree, who lost his car because a co-owner incurred ticket debt on a different vehicle. After the vehicle is impounded, moreover, forfeiture is a conse- quence only of the failure to pay, not the antecedent legal infraction. §9–100–120(f ). Those features strongly suggest that “the purpose of vehi cle impoundments” under Chi- cago’s scheme “is to collect a debt, not enforce public safety laws.” Pet. for Cert. 10. If so, then Tyler would seem to control, and the city’s failure to compensate owners for the loss of their vehicles would likely violate the Takings Clause. The city’s practice of surrendering cars to lienhold- ers or selling them for their scrap value, rather than at a fair auction, only amplifies the potential constitutional in- firmity. Cf. Pung v. Isabella County, 609 U. S. 30, 33 (2026) (just compensation is measured based on “fairly conducted” tax sale). Because of its mistaken reliance on Bennis, the Seventh Circuit considered Chicago’s ve hicle-forfeiture scheme “a ‘classic example’ ” of the State’s “police power.” 163 F. 4th, at 414 (quoting Hadley v. South Bend, 154 F. 4th 549, 556 (CA7 2025)). As I have previous ly written, the lower courts are divided over “the extent to which the Takings Clause applies to exercises of the police power.” Baker v. City of McKinney, 604 U. S. 1035, 1038 (2024) (statement of SOTOMAYOR, J., respecting denial of certiorari). Here, the Seventh Circuit embraced the expansive notion that “exer- cise[s] of the City’s police po wer to enforce its traffic code” are immune to takings claims. 163 F. 4th, at 414. Some 4 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. courts have likewise appeared to adopt a categorical rule that the Takings Clause does not apply when the govern- ment acts under any of its police powers. See, e.g., Amer- iSource Corp. v. United States, 525 F. 3d 1149, 1153 (CA Fed. 2008); Lech v. Jackson, 791 Fed. Appx. 711, 717 (CA10 2019). Others have held, more narrowly, that the just-com- pensation requirement is subject to a public-safety or ne - cessity exception, see, e.g., Baker v. McKinney , 84 F. 4th 378, 388 (CA5 2023); Pena v. Los Angeles, 158 F. 4th 1033, 1035 (CA9 2025), or that no property is taken when it is damaged incident to a lawful search or arrest, see, e .g., Slaybaugh v. Rutherford County, 114 F. 4th 593, 598 (CA6 2024); Hadley, 154 F. 4th, at 554; Pena, 158 F. 4th, at 1050 (Friedland, J., concurring in judgment). It is still an “open question” whether these or any other approaches are con - sistent with this Court’s precedents. Baker, 604 U. S., at 1038. Few of these decisions likewise explain the source of any such police-power exception to the Takings Clause— whether the common law, the Constitution, or elsewhere. Such questions thus continue to “benefit from further per- colation” in the lower courts before this Court chooses to in- tervene. Id., at 1039. Petitioners, moreover, have lodged a facial challenge to Chicago’s ordinance, which might re- quire this Court to invalidate even those features of the law that have nothing to do with vehicle forfeiture. See, e.g., §9–100–120(a) (providing for immobilization of vehicles). I therefore concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari. I none- theless write to emphasize that courts should carefully and narrowly define the circumstances in which the State’s ex - ercise of its police powers are held exempt from the just- compensation requirement, as well as explain the source of any such exemption. Where, as here, a person alleges a “classic taking in which the government directly appropri - ates private property for its own use” or to pay an outstand- ing debt, like a tax lien, Tyler, 598 U. S., at 639 (internal quotation marks omitted), the talismanic invocation of the 5 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. State’s “law enforcement authority,” 163 F. 4th, at 414, may be insufficient to avoid the requirement of just compensa- tion. I again encourage courts considering this issue to take care that due deference to state police powers does not eclipse constitutional rights.

The city then can do as it pleases with the vehicle, with no obligation to pay compensation, offset the unpaid ticket debt, or return any surplus to the owner if the vehicle is sold for a profit. See Chicago, Ill., Municipal Code §§9–100–120(b), (f ) (2026). The Seventh Circuit upheld that scheme as con- sistent with the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, rea- soning that it is “an exercise of the City’s police power to enforce its traffic code.” 163 F. 4th 411, 414 (2025). I have serious concerns about that conclusion, which implicates a Circuit split over whether, and under what circumstances, exercises of the State’s police power are immune to takings claims. Because that split would continue to benefit from further percolation, however, and because this case is not the best vehicle to resolve the split, I concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari. Chicago’s vehicle-forfeiture scheme is vast and lucrative, helping the city generate, according to one estimate, $264 million in traffic-ticket revenue (or 7 percent of the city’s operating budget) in 2016. See M. Sanchez & S. Kambham- pati, How Chicago Ticket Debt Sends Black Motorists Into Bankruptcy, ProPublica (Feb. 27, 2018), https://fea- tures.propublica.org/driven-into-debt/chicago-ticket-debt- 2 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. bankruptcy/ (archived at https:// perma.cc/K8MU-KVTW). Petitioners Ryan O’Donnell and Michael Goree are two of the many Chicago motorists sub - ject to that scheme. According to the complaint filed in this case, O’Donnell received two tickets for an expired meter and one ticket for time-restricted parking, totaling approx- imately $524. Goree did not have any tickets himself; ra- ther, a co-signer on his vehicle had approximately $560 of outstanding ticket debt from a different vehicle. After those tickets went unpaid, the city towed and impounded peti - tioners’ vehicles, adding additional boot, tow, and storage fees. It then sold O’Donnell’s vehicle for its scrap value of $273 and relinquished Goree’s vehicle to the lienholder. Neither petitioner received any compensation for the loss of their cars. Petitioners sued the city, alleging that its scheme facially violates the Takings Clause, which bars taking “private property” for “public use, without just compensation.” They asserted that §9–100–120 empowers the city to take vehi- cles “without providing any compensation to the owner or even a hearing to determine fair compensation.” Complaint in No. 1:23–cv–01192 (ND Ill.), ECF Doc. 1, ¶73. The Dis- trict Court dismissed the suit, see App. to Pet. for Cert. 16– 18; and the Seventh Circuit affirmed, see 163 F. 4th, at 414–415. As relevant here, the Seventh Circuit rejected pe- titioners’ argument that Ch icago’s vehicle-forfeiture scheme is like the tax-forfeiture statute this Court invali- dated in Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U. S. 631 (2023), for failure to return any surplus to the homeowner after a tax sale. The better analogy, the Seventh Circuit reasoned, was to Bennis v. Michigan, 516 U. S. 442 (1996), where this Court held that the government may seize property used in the violation of the law without providing any compensa- tion to the owner. See 163 F. 4th, at 414–415 (citing Bennis, 516 U. S., at 453); see also id., at 452 (forfeitures that 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. comport with due process do not trigger the duty of just compensation). Unlike the laws discussed in Bennis, however, Chicago does not impound only those vehicles involved in violations of its municipal traffic code. Rather, the city may impound any vehicle of a delinquent resident so long as ticket debts remain unpaid, regardless of whether the vehicle was in- volved in an infraction. §9–100–120(b). Indeed, that is pre- cisely what happened to Goree, who lost his car because a co-owner incurred ticket debt on a different vehicle. After the vehicle is impounded, moreover, forfeiture is a conse- quence only of the failure to pay, not the antecedent legal infraction. §9–100–120(f ). Those features strongly suggest that “the purpose of vehi cle impoundments” under Chi- cago’s scheme “is to collect a debt, not enforce public safety laws.” Pet. for Cert. 10. If so, then Tyler would seem to control, and the city’s failure to compensate owners for the loss of their vehicles would likely violate the Takings Clause. The city’s practice of surrendering cars to lienhold- ers or selling them for their scrap value, rather than at a fair auction, only amplifies the potential constitutional in- firmity. Cf. Pung v. Isabella County, 609 U. S. 30, 33 (2026) (just compensation is measured based on “fairly conducted” tax sale). Because of its mistaken reliance on Bennis, the Seventh Circuit considered Chicago’s ve hicle-forfeiture scheme “a ‘classic example’ ” of the State’s “police power.” 163 F. 4th, at 414 (quoting Hadley v. South Bend, 154 F. 4th 549, 556 (CA7 2025)). As I have previous ly written, the lower courts are divided over “the extent to which the Takings Clause applies to exercises of the police power.” Baker v. City of McKinney, 604 U. S. 1035, 1038 (2024) (statement of SOTOMAYOR, J., respecting denial of certiorari). Here, the Seventh Circuit embraced the expansive notion that “exer- cise[s] of the City’s police po wer to enforce its traffic code” are immune to takings claims. 163 F. 4th, at 414. Some 4 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. courts have likewise appeared to adopt a categorical rule that the Takings Clause does not apply when the govern- ment acts under any of its police powers. See, e.g., Amer- iSource Corp. v. United States, 525 F. 3d 1149, 1153 (CA Fed. 2008); Lech v. Jackson, 791 Fed. Appx. 711, 717 (CA10 2019). Others have held, more narrowly, that the just-com- pensation requirement is subject to a public-safety or ne - cessity exception, see, e.g., Baker v. McKinney , 84 F. 4th 378, 388 (CA5 2023); Pena v. Los Angeles, 158 F. 4th 1033, 1035 (CA9 2025), or that no property is taken when it is damaged incident to a lawful search or arrest, see, e .g., Slaybaugh v. Rutherford County, 114 F. 4th 593, 598 (CA6 2024); Hadley, 154 F. 4th, at 554; Pena, 158 F. 4th, at 1050 (Friedland, J., concurring in judgment). It is still an “open question” whether these or any other approaches are con - sistent with this Court’s precedents. Baker, 604 U. S., at 1038. Few of these decisions likewise explain the source of any such police-power exception to the Takings Clause— whether the common law, the Constitution, or elsewhere. Such questions thus continue to “benefit from further per- colation” in the lower courts before this Court chooses to in- tervene. Id., at 1039. Petitioners, moreover, have lodged a facial challenge to Chicago’s ordinance, which might re- quire this Court to invalidate even those features of the law that have nothing to do with vehicle forfeiture. See, e.g., §9–100–120(a) (providing for immobilization of vehicles). I therefore concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari. I none- theless write to emphasize that courts should carefully and narrowly define the circumstances in which the State’s ex - ercise of its police powers are held exempt from the just- compensation requirement, as well as explain the source of any such exemption. Where, as here, a person alleges a “classic taking in which the government directly appropri - ates private property for its own use” or to pay an outstand- ing debt, like a tax lien, Tyler, 598 U. S., at 639 (internal quotation marks omitted), the talismanic invocation of the 5 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. State’s “law enforcement authority,” 163 F. 4th, at 414, may be insufficient to avoid the requirement of just compensa- tion. I again encourage courts considering this issue to take care that due deference to state police powers does not eclipse constitutional rights.

documents.searchText: 1 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES JESUS HERRERA-SALAZAR v. UNITED STATES ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT No. 25–6989. Decided October 13, 2026 The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. Statement of J USTICE SOTOMAYOR, with whom J USTICE GORSUCH joins, respecting the denial of certiorari. Jesus Herrera-Salazar was indicted in 2020 on one count of being “found in” the United States following removal, in violation of 8 U. S. C. §1326(a). He pleaded guilty and served his term of imprisonment. While on supervised re - lease, during which he was expressly instructed not to leave the Eastern District of Oklahoma, Herrera-Salazar was pulled over in a traffic stop in Heavener, Oklahoma, and once again arrested and indicted under §1326(a). He was convicted by a jury and sentenced to new terms of impris- onment and supervised release. Because I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case. I write, however, to underscore the serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar. After being once convicted and punished for being found in the United States and, as part of his original sentence, prohibited from leaving the United States, Herrera-Salazar was convicted and punished for being found in the United States a second time. As an initial matter, it is not clear that the statutory language “found in . . . the United States” can fairly be read to encompass a person who has already been found by the Government and compelled to remain in the United States under Government supervision. Even as- suming that it can, however, Herrera-Salazar’s second 2 HERRERA-SALAZAR v. UNITED STATES Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. conviction is difficult to square with the Constitution’s ad- monition that no person shall “be subject for the same of- fence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.” Amdt. 5. As our precedents explain, “the Double Jeopardy Clause protects against a second prosecution for the same offense after conviction.” Currier v. Virginia, 585 U. S. 493, 501 (2018) (internal quotation marks omitted). The question in a case like this is what constitutes the “same offense.” In rejecting Herrera-Salazar’s double jeopardy objections, the Tenth Circuit looked to the text of §1326(a) to answer that question. It concluded that because the “‘allowable unit of prosecution’” did not require a separate predicate reentry for each violation of the statute, see Sanabria v. United States, 437 U. S. 54, 69 (1978), each of Herrera-Salazar’s prosecutions and convictions was for a separate offense. By those lights, with a single unlawful reentry supplying the necessary statutory predicate, a person in Herrera-Sala- zar’s shoes can be subjected to repeated, limitless “found in” charges without offending the Constitution. “The Double Jeopardy Clause is not such a fragile guar- antee that prosecutors can avoid its limitations by the sim- ple expedient of dividing a single crime into a series of tem- poral or spatial units.” Brown v. Ohio, 432 U. S. 161, 169 (1977). Yet that is just what the Government did here. Herrera-Salazar was convicted of “a crime which was con- tinuous, extending over the whole period” he was present in the United States after his previous removal and reentry. In re Nielsen, 131 U. S. 176, 187 (1889). That continuous crime plainly could not have concluded until the Govern- ment allowed Herrera-Salazar to leave the country. Be - cause the crime of being found in the United States was thus still ongoing at the time of his second arrest, the Gov- ernment’s theory rests on the premise that Herrera-Salazar could be charged, convicted, and punished twice solely “be- cause the charges against him focused on different parts of ” his compelled continuous presence in the United States. 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. Brown, 432 U. S., at 169 (recognizing a double jeopardy vi - olation where the petitioner faced two charges based on two points of time within a continuous “9-day joyride”). When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves continuous, uninterrupted conduct, our precedents and the logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that the Government is barred from charging that defendant with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by focusing on a different time marker. That makes sense. Were it otherwise, there might be “ ‘an indictment covering each of the . . . months’ ” of the continuous crime, “ ‘or even an indictment covering every week.’ ” In re Nielsen , 131 U. S., at 186. There is even more force to this double jeop- ardy objection where the Government itself effectively for- bids the defendant to cease his unlawful conduct. Here, in- deed, the Government might have charged Herrera-Salazar with a separate violation of §1326(a) for each day that he was “found in” prison while serving his sentence for the first conviction. Absurd as that seems, it is a logical outgrowth of the Government’s contention that Herrera-Salazar’s sec- ond §1326(a) conviction poses no double jeopardy problem. * * * From the moment he was released from custody after serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera-Salazar was presented with a Hobson’s choice. In the Government’s eyes, whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law. While Herrera-Salazar was caught in this bind, the Government prosecuted and punished him yet again for being “found in” the United States, even though all agree he was forbidden to leave the United States. Should circumstances like these arise again, I en - courage courts to avoid the constitutional absurdity that oc- curred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning.

UNITED STATES ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT No. 25–6989. Decided October 13, 2026 The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. Statement of J USTICE SOTOMAYOR, with whom J USTICE GORSUCH joins, respecting the denial of certiorari. Jesus Herrera-Salazar was indicted in 2020 on one count of being “found in” the United States following removal, in violation of 8 U. S. C. §1326(a). He pleaded guilty and served his term of imprisonment. While on supervised re - lease, during which he was expressly instructed not to leave the Eastern District of Oklahoma, Herrera-Salazar was pulled over in a traffic stop in Heavener, Oklahoma, and once again arrested and indicted under §1326(a). He was convicted by a jury and sentenced to new terms of impris- onment and supervised release. Because I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case. I write, however, to underscore the serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar. After being once convicted and punished for being found in the United States and, as part of his original sentence, prohibited from leaving the United States, Herrera-Salazar was convicted and punished for being found in the United States a second time. As an initial matter, it is not clear that the statutory language “found in . . . the United States” can fairly be read to encompass a person who has already been found by the Government and compelled to remain in the United States under Government supervision. Even as- suming that it can, however, Herrera-Salazar’s second 2 HERRERA-SALAZAR v. UNITED STATES Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. conviction is difficult to square with the Constitution’s ad - monition that no person shall “be subject for the same of - fence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.” Amdt. 5. As our precedents explain, “the Double Jeopardy Clause protects against a second prosecution for the same offense after conviction.” Currier v. Virginia, 585 U. S. 493, 501 (2018) (internal quotation marks omitted). The question in a case like this is what constitutes the “same offense.” In rejecting Herrera-Salazar’s double jeopardy objections, the Tenth Circuit looked to the text of §1326(a) to answer that question. It concluded that because the “‘allowable unit of prosecution’ ” did not require a separate predicate reentry for each violation of the statute, see Sanabria v. United States, 437 U. S. 54, 69 (1978), each of Herrera- Salazar’s prosecutions and convictions was for a separate offense. By those lights, with a single unlawful reentry supplying the necessary statutory predicate, a person in Herrera -Sala- zar’s shoes can be subjected to repeated, limitless “found in” charges without offending the Constitution. “The Double Jeopardy Clause is not such a fragile guar - antee that prosecutors can avoid its limitations by the sim- ple expedient of dividing a single crime into a series of tem- poral or spatial units.” Brown v. Ohio, 432 U. S. 161, 169 (1977). Yet that is just what the Government did here. Herrera-Salazar was convicted of “a crime which was con- tinuous, extending over the whole period” he was present in the United States after his previous removal and reentry. In re Nielsen, 131 U. S. 176, 187 (1889). That continuous crime plainly could not have concluded until the Govern - ment allowed Herrera -Salazar to leave the country. Be - cause the crime of being found in the United States was thus still ongoing at the time of his second arrest, the Gov- ernment’s theory rests on the premise that Herrera-Salazar could be charged, convicted, and punished twice solely “be- cause the charges against him focused on different parts of ” his compelled continuous presence in the United States. 3 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. Brown, 432 U. S., at 169 (recognizing a double jeopardy vi- olation where the petitioner faced two charges based on two points of time within a continuous “9-day joyride”). When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves continuous, uninterrupted conduct, our precedents and the logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that the Government is barred from charging that defendant with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by focusing on a different time marker. That makes sense. Were it otherwise, there might be “‘an indictment covering each of the . . . months’” of the continuous crime, “‘or even an indictment covering every week.’” In re Nielsen, 131 U. S., at 186. There is even more force to this double jeop - ardy objection where the Government itself effectively for - bids the defendant to cease his unlawful conduct. Here, in- deed, the Government might have charged Herrera-Salazar with a separate v iolation of §1326(a) for each day that he was “found in” prison while serving his sentence for the first conviction. Absurd as that seems, it is a logical outgrowth of the Government’s contention that Herrera-Salazar’s sec- ond §1326(a) conviction poses no double jeopardy problem. * * * From the moment he was released from custody after serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera -Salazar was presented with a Hobson’s choice. In the Government’s eyes, whether Herrera -Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law. While Herrera -Salazar was caught in this bind, the Government prosecuted and punished him yet again for being “found in” the United States, even though all agree he was forbidden to leave the United States. Shou ld circumstances like these arise again, I en - courage courts to avoid the constitutional absurdity that oc- curred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning.

Statement of J USTICE SOTOMAYOR respecting the denial of certiorari. The right to an impartial jury, embedded both in the Sixth Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, is fundamental to our system of justice. See Gray v. Mississippi , 481 U. S. 648, 657 (1987); Gomez v. United States, 490 U. S. 858, 876 (1989). It is the role of a judge to protect, not endanger, that impartiality. In this case, during jury selection for a capital murder trial, the trial judge held a potential juror in contempt for being 30 minutes late to court and ordered him arrested. Those or - ders were issued in front of the remaining pool of potential jurors. After the judge ordered the tardy juror arrested, two po- tential jurors, who were questioned individually during voir dire, expressed fear of sharing their views about the case. One potential juror asked, after the judge inquired about his unwillingness to recommend the death penalty, “Will I be charged or thrown in jail?” 6 Record 409. An- other, after being asked whether he was willing to consider mitigating factors in decidi ng whether to recommend a death sentence, stated: “Well, I kind of based [my opinion] on what the Judge told me, because I don’t want to get in trouble for my beliefs.” 7 id., at 482. Although the judge assured these jurors that they would not be punished for sharing their views, this assurance was given during the individual questioning and not in the presence of the rest of 2 MULKEY v. ALABAMA Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. the jury pool. It is unknown how many other potential ju- rors felt similarly but did not share their fear because they were not called for individual questioning. This case comes to us on plain-error review because no objection to the judge’s conduct was raised below. Because that posture limits the scope of our review, I concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari. I write, however, to highlight that this case provides an example of why judges should re- strain themselves from conducting any proceedings that are collateral to the trial in front of a jury. The record here amply de monstrates how a judge’s con- duct can have a profoundly negative impact on members of the jury pool. Such conduct may affect not only what poten- tial jurors are willing to say in front of the judge, but also whether they will apply thei r independent judgment in- stead of following what they perceive the judge may person- ally think. See, e.g., Starr v. United States , 153 U. S. 614, 626 (1894). If potential jurors are not comfortable express- ing their own views, voir dire’s “critical function” of identi- fying and removing prospective jurors who cannot be im- partial is undermined. Rosales-Lopez v. United States, 451 U. S. 182, 188 (1981) (plurality opinion). “The influence of the voir dire process,” moreover, “may persist through the whole course of the trial proceedings.” Powers v. Ohio, 499 U. S. 400, 412 (1991). This danger is especially acute in a capital case such as this one, where the defendant’s life hangs in the balance. To guard against it, judges should limit exposing a jury to collateral proceedings, particularly when those proceedings might frighten or intimidate the jury.
